units.translation: d. From Cecropia: 〈...〉 Creusa, Orithyia, Procris; and of Orithyia, Chione, Chthonia, Cleopatra, Zetes and Calais. Boreas, seeing Orithyia playing by the Ilissus, fell in love with her; from her these were born.
1 Κεκροπίηθεν as a new lemma W | W preferred to indicate a lacuna | 7 Ἀστικῆς Holstenius : Ἀττικῆς in L : Θράκης in PA | Σαπαϊκῆς K, cf. W 31
e. From Cecropia: the acropolis of Attica was formerly called Cecropia. Lm (P)
f. 〈Of the Ilissus:〉 a river of Attica. Lg

216-17a. Sarpedonian rock: a city of Attica named after Sarpedon, king of Thrace, brother of Poltys. 〈Beside the stream of the river Erginus:〉 he added this because there is also another Sarpedonian rock in Cilicia.
8 Apollodorus, Library II 105 | 9 sch. c with similar passages | 12 sch. II 1120 | sch. B rec. Γ 95
8 Σαρπηδόνος in P : -ήδοντος in L | 9 supplied by W | τοῦτο δὲ in L : τὰ δὲ ἐφεξῆς in P
b. 〈Of Erginus:〉 a river of Thrace. Lg
218. λυγαίοις: dark, by metonymy; for λύγος means darkness, from the plant λύγος, which is dense and thick. LmP
13 after σκότος A adds ἀφ’ οὗ καὶ λύγη (ἠλύγη ?) νὺξ ἡ σκοτεινή | λύγου in P : -ος in L

219-20. On the tips of their feet: on their ankles or heels. And ἐρεμνάς, by syncope for ἐρεβεννάς, that is, properly dark, hence black. The sense: they shook their black wings as they moved, terrifying to behold.
15 Apollonius, Homeric Lexicon 75 | Hesychius ἐρεμνή | Etymologicum Orionis 52, 9 | Etymologicum Magnum 370 | Etymologicum Gudianum 519 | Eustathius 460
15 τὰς in P : omitted in L : 〈τοῦ〉 K | 16 deleted by W | ὁ δὲ λόγος and following W traced back | 17 μελαίνας W : μικράς in L : δικράς in P : ἐρυμνάς in F
221-22. φολίδεσσι: with the spots, the variegated markings of the wings. 〈κράατος〉 ὑπάτοιο: of the top of the head.
19 added by Steph. | ὑπάτοιο the same : -ηε in L : -ου in P
224-26a. Nor even the son of him himself: Acastus, son of Pelias, married Cretheis or, as some say, Hippolyte. She fell in love with Peleus
20 Hesiod fragment 78 Rz.2 | sch. Pindar, Nemean IV 92a | sch. Aristophanes, Clouds 1063 | Apollodorus, Library III 164 ff.

224/26a. and demanded to lie with him. When she failed, she accused Peleus to her husband, claiming that he wanted to lie with her. He took Peleus hunting on Pelion and left him unarmed, so that he would be killed by wild beasts. But Hermes appeared, or, as some say, Chiron, and gave him a Hephaestus-made knife. Killing the beasts he encountered, he returned to the city and killed Acastus himself and Acastus' wife.
